transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-01-22 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~48m
Location: Zoom (recording)
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Rahul Desai (Redwood SE), Lina Park (Redwood SE), Mark Liu (CTO, Helix), Dana Park (Lead ML Eng), Evan Sorensen (Platform Eng)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
Helix is evaluating Redwood for a mixed deployment: hosted for early experiments, Dedicated or Private for regulatory workloads. Key integration questions: SDK support (Python/Node), LangChain / LlamaIndex connectors, running a gateway/proxy in front of Redwood, per-route rate limits and quotas, observability hooks (tracing, per-request cost), and security controls (KMS, SSO, audit logs). They requested SOC2 and an integration guide; asked to run a benchmark/pilot.

Topics covered:
- high-level product fit (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
- SDKs and open-source integration (LangChain, LlamaIndex)
- gateway/proxy patterns and local caching (KV cache / prefix caching)
- rate limiting, quotas, token accounting
- observability: traces, per-model latency/cost dashboards, hooks for Datadog/Sentry
- security: SSO, RBAC, KMS, audit logs, data residency

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intros — I'll hand off to Rahul for the technical part but first, what are you hoping to cover today?
[00:15] Mark (Helix): Yeah, thanks. We're evaluating options for inference across a few product teams. Short story: we want hosted for fast experiments, but ultimately some workloads will need dedicated or private because of GDPR and vendor controls. Today it's mostly about integration patterns and limits.
[00:30] Rahul (Redwood SE): Great, that's what we've been hearing a lot. Can you tell us a bit about your stack — are you using LangChain or Llama index, what does the gateway look like, and any latency SLOs?
[00:45] Dana (Helix): We're prototyping with LangChain and LlamaIndex — well, Llama index in one team, long chain in another (laughs), but yes LangChain primarily. We also have an internal API gateway (kong-ish) that routes to external services. We need to know if we should call Redwood directly from services or put a proxy in front.
[01:15] Lina (Redwood SE): Totally. Common patterns: direct SDK calls from backend (Python/Node SDK), or a lightweight gateway/proxy that handles auth, retries, and rate limiting. Both are supported. If you run a local gateway you can keep fine-grained control but you lose some of the built-in Redwood quota enforcement unless you mirror it.
[01:40] Evan (Helix): Our platform team prefers a single outbound egress point; running a proxy is easier for compliance. Concern is we don't want to double-count tokens or lose streaming efficiency.
[02:05] Rahul: Good note — streaming works fine through a proxy, but you have to forward chunked responses and keep connection timeouts tuned. Token accounting is server-side at Redwood; if you proxy, we still count tokens on our side, so your billing / per-route quota mappings should be done with headers or API keys.
[02:30] Mark: How do API keys map to teams? We want per-team quotas and per-model routing — e.g., low-cost model for bulk embeddings, higher quality for chat.
[02:45] Sofia: We support API keys at org/team level in Hosted; Dedicated adds more granular routing and per-route SLOs. You can set per-key rate limits and quotas in the console, and also have automated fallback routing to cheaper variants if the sler — the SLO breach occurs.
[03:00] Dana: When you say "Dedicated" are we getting isolated GPU pools? We need to know about throughput guarantees and if we can pin model versions for reproducible outputs.
[03:20] Rahul: Dedicated is reserved capacity — yes, isolated pools and you can pin model versions. SLA-backed throughput and latency targets are available in the contract. Private (VPC/on-prem) adds the control plane in your network and lets you bring your own KMS.
[03:40] Mark: KMS — important. For private workloads we need HSM-level key control. Do you integrate with common KMS providers?
[03:50] Lina: Yes, we integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS and support external HSM/Bring-Your-Own-Key in Private. We'll send the KMS integration docs in the follow-up.
[04:10] Evan: OK. On the SDK side — what's the maturity? We need Python and Node samples, and LangChain connectors ideally.
[04:25] Rahul: Our SDKs support Python and Node in GA. LangChain connectors exist and are maintained; LlamaIndex (sometimes mis-typed as llama index) integrations are community-backed but we have sample repos. We also have a drop-in API compatible with common provider adapters.
[04:45] Dana: Any gotchas with LangChain agents or memory store when using Redwood? Specifically with KV cache and embeddings?
[05:00] Rahul: Two notes — Redwood runtime has an internal KV cache for prefix caching which reduces cost for repeated context; that interacts nicely with LangChain's memory layers but you should be explicit about where you keep long-term vector stores (we don't store long-term unless configured). For embeddings, we recommend separate per-tenant embedding keys and quotas.
[05:30] Mark: Rate limits and quotas — we need per-route and per-API-key limits and also global org quotas. Can you throttle at the model or route level?
[05:45] Lina: Yes. Hosted supports per-key rate limits, per-route quotas, and token-based budgeting. Dedicated gives more control and can enforce limits at the capacity pool. You can set hard limits and soft throttles. Also can configure burst windows.
[06:10] Evan: How about observability — we use Datadog and Sentry. We need trace IDs, per-request latency and token cost breakdowns, and the ability to ingest logs into our SIEM.
[06:30] Rahul: Redwood exposes request-level metadata: request id, model, tokens-in/out, latency. We have webhook export, direct Datadog metrics, and an OpenTelemetry hook so traces can be correlated. Audit logs are available for Dedicated/Private; hosted has enriched logs for higher tiers.
[07:00] Dana: Can the console give per-route cost breakdowns so product teams can see spend by feature?
[07:15] Sofia: Yes, the console has token-level cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and you can tag routes for chargeback. We'll demo that in the next call.
[07:30] Mark: Security questions — SOC2? SSO? RBAC?
[07:40] Lina: We're SOC 2 Type II certified. We support SSO via SAML and OIDC, fine-grained RBAC, and audit logs. For Private we'll support your own IdP behind your VPC. I'll attach SOC2 and SSO docs.
[08:00] Evan: Data residency — some customers mandate EU-only processing. Is that possible on Hosted?
[08:10] Rahul: Yes — we have region routing rules. Hosted can pin traffic to EU regions; Dedicated/Private obviously gives you control over location. There are nuances around backups and logs which we can walk through in the security packet.
[08:30] Mark: On benchmarking — we plan to run latency and cost tests. What does Redwood recommend for a trial to compare hosted vs dedicated?
[08:45] Rahul: We usually do a two-stage trial: 1) run a 1–2 week hosted pilot using your dev traffic, run LangChain workflows, measure latency/cost and correctness; 2) if you want dedicated, run a short capacity benchmark on a reserved pool with your real sequences and concurrency. Redwood SEs can help set up the harness.
[09:10] Dana: For the benchmark we'll need examples for prompt templates and metrics to capture — throughput, p99 latency, token cost per turn, model hallucination rate.
[09:25] Lina: We'll share a benchmark checklist and a sample harness (k6 + python clients) that measures those metrics.
[09:40] Mark: About running a gateway — if we put a proxy, can we cache embeddings or responses at the proxy to reduce calls?
[09:55] Rahul: You can cache results at the proxy; important to be careful with PII. For prefix caching and KV caching, Redwood's runtime does server-side caching which is more efficient for KV cache hits. Proxy-level caching is useful for deterministic calls like embeddings or reranking.
[10:20] Evan: Any notes about function calling or tool calls? We use tool-calls in LangChain agents.
[10:30] Rahul: Supported — streaming + function/tool calling is supported. You should forward chunked responses through your proxy. For function calling we recommend keeping the tool execution in your infra and passing structured outputs back to the model as needed.
[11:00] Dana: Do you have rate limits on streaming connections? We plan many long-lived streams for chat.
[11:10] Lina: We have connection limits per key and concurrency quotas. For high concurrency use Dedicated and tune the pool size. We'll share recommended timeouts and keepalive settings.
[11:40] Mark: What about model variants and automatic fallback? If our primary model is overloaded, can requests fall back to a cheaper variant automatically?
[11:55] Rahul: Yes, smart routing supports fallback policy. You can set model families and fallback chains. This is configurable per-route.
[12:10] Evan: Any gotchas around tokenization differences that affect pricing when moving between models?
[12:25] Lina: Tokenization differences exist; we include model-specific token accounting in the console. When comparing cost across models, normalize by tokenization and output length.
[12:40] Mark: Logs and auditing — how long are logs kept, and can we increase retention?
[12:50] Lina: Hosted has default retention windows; we offer add-ons for extended retention and export to your S3 or SIEM for Dedicated/Private.
[13:10] Dana: Ok let's talk timeline and stakeholders — procurement and legal will need security docs; engineering will want the repo and a test. We are targeting a pilot in Q1.
[13:28] Sofia: Great. We'll send the security packet and the LangChain example repo. Can we tentatively schedule a benchmark session for Feb 2?
[13:40] Mark: Feb 2 works. Procurement will start around mid-Feb once they see the pilot results.
[13:52] Evan: One more technical thing — do you support websocket streaming directly or only HTTP chunking?
[14:00] Rahul: We support both streaming over HTTP chunked and websockets in certain clients. SDKs handle streaming semantics for Node/Python.
[14:15] Dana: For embeddings we want deterministic outputs — is versioning sufficient to guarantee that?
[14:25] Lina: Pinning a specific model version helps. Also, ensure you pin any tokenizer and sampling params. We'll include a reproducibility section in the guide.
[14:40] Mark: Any reference customers doing similar flows?
[14:50] Sofia: We can share references in fintech and healthcare that use a hybrid Hosted/Dedicated approach; I'll drop a short list.
[15:05] Dana: Regarding LangChain connectors — are you upstreaming changes? We sometimes need custom retrievers.
[15:15] Rahul: We maintain provider adapters and upstream connectors; custom retrievers are usually implemented in your stack but we can help with examples.
[15:28] Mark: For Dedicated, what's the procurement cadence — minimum commitment?
[15:35] Sofia: There are monthly and annual reserved capacity options. We'll send the pricing matrix in the follow-up.
[15:50] Evan: A question about observability hooks — can we tag requests with product feature names for cost attribution?
[15:58] Lina: Yes — you can send metadata/tags on requests that get surfaced in dashboards. Also via header mapping if using a gateway.
[16:18] Dana: Any security concerns with forwarding user data to Hosted?
[16:25] Rahul: Standard: redact PII where possible, use dedicated keys, use private for regulated data, and enforce contract/data processing agreements. We'll provide specifics in the security packet.
[16:40] Mark: Great; can we recap next steps?
[16:45] Sofia: Sure — action items: we'll send SOC2 + KMS docs, LangChain/LlamaIndex sample repo, benchmark harness, and pricing for Dedicated. We'll also set the Feb 2 benchmark.
[16:58] Mark: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[17:05] (meeting ends)

Notes about transcription quality: occasional mis-recognition (e.g., LongChain for LangChain). Speaker attribution is mostly correct but may have small errors.
